raw_text:
### Introduction

Transcatheter structural heart interventions, most notably transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), have revolutionized the management of valvular heart disease [1]. For the majority of patients, transfemoral (TF) arterial access serves as the gold-standard route due to its minimally invasive nature and superior clinical outcomes [2]. However, approximately 5% to 10% of patients present with severe peripheral artery disease, critical iliofemoral caliber mismatch, severe calcification, or extreme vessel tortuosity that precludes safe transfemoral retrograde delivery [3,4]. In the early eras of TAVR, surgical alternative approaches such as transapical or direct transaortic access were utilized [5]. However, these transthoracic approaches are highly invasive and associated with increased rates of perioperative morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and excess mortality [6]. Over the last decade, non-thoracic alternative percutaneous access routes have emerged, including transaxillary, transcarotid, and the highly innovative transfemoral transcaval (caval-aortic) approach [7,8].

### The Transcaval Concept and Physiology

Transcaval access involves creating a temporary tract between the retroperitoneal abdominal aorta and the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC) [9]. While intentionally forming an aortocaval fistula is counterintuitive to traditional vascular principles, its safety is supported by basic retroperitoneal fluid dynamics [10]. Because the hydrostatic pressure in the surrounding retroperitoneal space exceeds the venous pressure in the IVC, any arterial blood leaking from the aorta is decompressed directly and harmlessly back into the low-pressure venous circulation rather than accumulating as an expanding retroperitoneal hematoma [11]. This physiological phenomenon was first validated in a preclinical swine model in 2013 [11] and subsequently translated to the first-in-human clinical experience by Greenbaum et al. in 2014 [12]. By avoiding open thoracic incisions and preserving femoral-like ergonomics, transcaval access allows procedures to be performed under conscious sedation, minimizing the surgical and anesthetic burden on highly comorbid patients [13,14].

### Preprocedural CT Planning and Patient Selection

Meticulous preprocedural planning utilizing multi-slice computed tomography (CT) is the single most critical determinant of transcaval success [15]. Society guidelines and clinical protocols dictate that CT angiography must be evaluated to identify a calcium-free "window" on the right lateral wall of the infrarenal aorta [16,17]. This target must be directly adjacent to the IVC, free of any interposed anatomical structures such as the small bowel, duodenum, or major retroperitoneal lymph nodes [17]. Crucially, the target window must be positioned at a safe distance (ideally >15 mm) from the renal arteries and the aortoiliac bifurcation to preserve landing zones for potential bailout covered stents should closure complications arise [18]. Recent technical modifications include the use of intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-assisted aorta-outward puncture to optimize trajectory selection in complex, calcified anatomies [18].

### Procedural Technique and Large-Bore Crossing

The transcaval procedure is executed in a specialized hybrid catheterization laboratory [19]. Under fluoroscopic guidance, a customized venous crossing catheter is advanced from the femoral vein and positioned in the IVC opposite the aortic target [19,20]. Utilizing transcatheter electrosurgery, a standard 0.014-inch guidewire is electrified using radiofrequency energy from a standard electrosurgical generator [21,22]. This energy vaporizes a microscopic channel through the walls of the IVC and aorta, allowing the wire to easily traverse the tissue planes into a snare pre-positioned in the aorta via a secondary arterial access [22]. Once captured, the wire is exchanged for a high-support guidewire, enabling the sequential dilation of the tract and insertion of a large-caliber introducer sheath (typically 14–22 Fr) [23]. To optimize safety and reduce access-site complications, operators have increasingly adopted transradial secondary arterial access to guide both the intervention and subsequent tract closure [24].

### Clinical Applications and Expanding Indications

Although initially developed to facilitate large-bore TAVR in patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis [25], the utility of transcaval access has expanded dramatically. It has been successfully employed to treat native pure aortic regurgitation using dedicated locator-based, self-expanding devices [26]. Furthermore, transcaval access can be combined with complex leaflet modification techniques, such as bioprosthetic aortic scallop intentional laceration (BASILICA), during valve-in-valve interventions to prevent iatrogenic coronary obstruction [27]. Beyond TAVR, this access route has become an invaluable tool for the percutaneous delivery of large-bore mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices. Notably, it facilitates the percutaneous insertion of the 23 Fr Impella 5.0 microaxial flow pump in patients with cardiogenic shock and prohibitive peripheral vascular disease, avoiding surgical cutdowns and associated ischemic limb complications [28]. Additionally, it has been used to deliver large endografts for percutaneous endovascular aneurysm repairs (EVAR/TEVAR) [29].

### Tract Closure and Clinical Outcomes

Upon completion of the primary structural intervention, the transcaval tract is closed from the venous side using a nitinol occlusion device, most commonly the Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO-1) [30]. The pivotal, prospective, multicenter National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) trial demonstrated a 99% access success rate and a 98% device closure success rate [2]. Long-term 12-month follow-up confirmed that the residual aortocaval shunts are hemodynamically benign and typically undergo spontaneous thrombosis and complete closure over time [3]. Large-scale registry data comparing contemporary alternative routes suggest that transcaval access is associated with significantly lower rates of stroke compared to transaxillary access (2.5% vs. 13.2%), with equivalent rates of major bleeding and vascular complications [4]. As operator experience matures and dedicated transcaval closure devices enter the clinical arena, this approach is poised to solidify its role as the premier non-thoracic alternative access for complex structural heart interventions.
